doc.title: Derek Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995

title: Advice to young musicians
summary: Smith urges playing with better players, learning the business and publishing, and avoiding shortcuts.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Well do you have any last words for our young jazz people at school, or Mike do you have something?

Yeah. I wanted to just ask you if you could give a word to young people, college age people, that you know are going to see this interview in years to come. If you could give them just a piece of advice about listening to and participating in or appreciating this music. Any hints? Any insights that would help them get handles on it, quickly and easily?
Well of course it’s different than when I was a kid. There weren’t all these music programs at colleges for one thing. When I grew up there was two colleges, Oxford and

Cambridge. And you had to be brilliant to get into there. And they certainly didn’t have a jazz program. But now you can go to college — almost any major college now has got a jazz program. I’m sure they vary, some are better than others. But there are some that are really very good. And so a kid with talent, if they can possibly afford to get there on a scholarship or something, should go to one of these and soak up as much information as they can. But like we were talking about before, it’s not really the information it’s the talent and managing to bring it out. Now my own experience has been you can only do that by playing with players. I always try and make it a point, always try to play with people who are better than you, because that’s the way you’re going to learn. And not just playing, but hanging around, talking to them. There’s so much to talk about, especially the older players, you know somebody like Milt to talk to. I mean Milt’s the greatest guy in an airplane on a long plane ride, because he’s got so many stories. Some are funny, some are cogent, some are—that’s great for young people to hear. I don’t think there are any shortcuts. You’ve got to keep playing your instrument, keep learning. I always tell them, you know, for business reasons, learn to write, learn to sing, learn all the angles of the business, which I didn’t learn until I was much older. Learn about publishing. You know publishers make all the money.
Sometimes the artist is the last one to see his money am I right?

Absolutely. We create it but it’s a business. And learn that it’s a business. I think kids know that today. They’re much hipper about it. But I kind of regret that I was much older before I found out things like that, I wasn’t into it. I just wanted to play, I wanted to play. And I can’t play this thing that I hear in my head, I’ve got to keep playing. But I don’t think there are any shortcuts. I don’t know whether that was Clark Terry’s words but he says first you imitate, then you assimilate, and lastly then you [innovate]. It’s wonderful really and I don’t find any shortcuts. Just keep playing and try to play with people that are better than you all the time.
